title: Of the Roman grandeur
paragraphs: I will only say a word or two on this enormous subject, to show the simplicity of those who compare the pitiful greatness of our times with that of Rome. In the seventh book of Cicero's Familiar Letters — and let the grammarians strike out the surname "familiar" if they wish, for it is in truth not very appropriate; and those who, instead of "familiar", have substituted "ad Familiares" can find something to back them up in what Suetonius says in his Life of Caesar, that there was a volume of letters of his "ad Familiares" — there is one addressed to Caesar, then in Gaul, in which Cicero repeats these words from the end of an earlier letter Caesar had sent him: "As for Marcus Furius, whom you have recommended to me, I will make him king of Gaul, and if you want me to promote any other friend of yours, send him to me." It was nothing new for a simple Roman citizen, as Caesar then was, to dispose of kingdoms — for he stripped his kingdom from King Deiotarus to give it to a gentleman of the city of Pergamum, called Mithridates; and those who wrote his Life record several cities sold by him; and Suetonius says he once received from King Ptolemy three million six hundred thousand crowns, which was very like selling him his own kingdom:
"Tot Galatae, tot Pontus, tot Lydia, nummis."
["So much for Galatia, so much for Pontus, so much for Lydia." — Claudius in Eutrop., i. 203.]

Mark Antony said that the greatness of the Roman people was visible not so much in what they took as in what they gave away — and indeed some ages before Antony they had dethroned a king with such astonishing authority that in all of Roman history I have seen nothing that more clearly shows the height of their power. Antiochus held all of Egypt, and was on the point of conquering Cyprus and other appendages of that empire. While he was in the midst of his victories, C. Popilius arrived from the Senate, and at their first meeting refused to take his hand until he had first read his letters. When the king had read them and said he would consider them, Popilius drew a circle around him with his cane and said: "Give me an answer to take back to the Senate before you step out of this circle." Antiochus, astonished at the bluntness of so peremptory an order, paused a moment and then replied: "I will obey the Senate's command." Then Popilius greeted him as a friend of the Roman people. To renounce his claim to so great a monarchy and so successful a course of conquest, from the effect of three lines in writing! He had reason, as he afterwards did, to send word to the Senate by his ambassadors that he had received their order with the same reverence as if it had come from the immortal gods.

All the kingdoms Augustus gained by right of war he either restored to those who had lost them or presented to strangers. And Tacitus, on this subject, speaking of Cogidunus, king of Britain, gives us, with a marvellous touch, an instance of that infinite power: the Romans, he says, had from earliest antiquity been accustomed to leave the kings they had subdued in possession of their kingdoms under their own authority,
["That they might have even kings to be their slaves." — Livy, xlv. 13.]

It is likely that Suleiman, whom we have seen make a gift of Hungary and other principalities, had this consideration more in mind than the one he was in the habit of giving — that he was sated and overloaded with so many monarchies and so much dominion, won by his own valour and that of his ancestors.
